_run.confidence_overall: HIGH for legal frameworks; MEDIUM for Ontario-specific regulatory details

hipaa.framework_summary: HIPAA applies to Covered Entities (healthcare providers, insurers, clearinghouses) and their Business Associates. A BA is any person/entity that creates, receives, maintains, or transmits PHI on behalf of a CE.
hipaa.ba_definition_trigger: Creates, receives, MAINTAINS, or transmits PHI — even without viewing it.
hipaa.mere_conduit_exception: Entities that transport PHI without persistent storage or routine access qualify as 'mere conduits' — NOT Business Associates. Example: postal carriers, ISPs handling encrypted packets in transit.

findings.claim: LocalWeb does not need a BAA because it never receives PHI
findings.rationale: The architectural claim is plausible: if only a status code (not PHI) is returned from the pharmacy API, and LocalWeb Workers are stateless, the BA definition is not triggered. However, two risks exist: (1) The Rx number + DOB combination may constitute PHI if it can identify an individual — HHS and many attorneys treat Rx numbers as PHI-adjacent. (2) HHS OCR's 2024 tracking technology guidance means ANY analytics pixel, heatmap tool, or third-party script on a healthcare site may create BA obligations for the tracking vendor.
findings.hhs_source: HHS.gov Business Associates FAQ; HHS OCR March 2024 Tracking Technologies Guidance
findings.required_action: Obtain legal opinion (healthcare attorney) confirming Rx number alone — without name, drug, or clinical data — falls outside PHI definition in this specific use pattern. Document this in the architectural attestation.
findings.risk_level: MEDIUM — architecture is sound; documentation is the gap

findings.claim: HIPAA-ready website frontend can exist without BAA if PHI never reaches it
findings.rationale: HHS guidance is clear: a BAA is not required with vendors whose services do not involve use or disclosure of PHI. A pure frontend serving static HTML/CSS/JS that has zero contact with PHI does not trigger BA definition. LocalWeb's static site + Cloudflare Worker architecture, where the Worker only receives a status code, is architecturally consistent with this.
findings.hhs_source: HHS.gov — Covered Entities and Business Associates guidance
findings.required_action: Maintain written architectural attestation. Do not add analytics tools (Google Analytics, Meta Pixel, Hotjar) to healthcare pages without legal review — these can create BA obligations.
findings.risk_level: LOW — if architecture maintained as documented

findings.claim: Marketing claim: 'HIPAA-ready websites'
findings.rationale: The term 'HIPAA-ready' is not a legal certification or regulated term. It is commonly used in the industry to mean 'architected to avoid triggering HIPAA obligations' or 'eligible for HIPAA-covered deployments.' LocalWeb CAN use this language IF it is accompanied by clear disclosure that (a) HIPAA compliance ultimately rests with the Covered Entity, (b) LocalWeb does not handle PHI, (c) the claim is architectural not certified. Without disclosures, 'HIPAA-ready' is potentially misleading.
findings.required_action: Add explicit disclosure language to all marketing materials. See Gap Analysis section for recommended disclosure text.
findings.risk_level: MEDIUM — reputational and potential FTC concern if claim is read as certification

findings.claim: Cloudflare is HIPAA-eligible and can be configured accordingly
findings.rationale: Cloudflare offers a HIPAA-eligible service tier with a BAA for Business Associates who handle PHI. LocalWeb's standard tier does not require this because PHI does not pass through. If a client's legal team requires Cloudflare to be covered, upgrade is available.
findings.source: Cloudflare Trust Hub — GDPR and HIPAA documentation
findings.risk_level: LOW — upgrade path exists

findings.claim: Heatmap aggregate data (timestamps + wait durations) is non-PHI
findings.rationale: Aggregate queue timing data without patient identifiers does not constitute PHI under HIPAA. Wait time + timestamp cannot be linked to an individual. This is analogous to web server access logs (IP + timestamp), which HHS does not classify as PHI in aggregate anonymous form.
findings.caveat: If timestamps could be reverse-correlated to identify a patient (e.g., 'only one patient was in Zone 2 at 2:47pm'), risk increases. For pharmacies with very low traffic, this is a theoretical concern.
findings.risk_level: LOW for most deployments

certification_path.real_hipaa_seal: No government-issued 'HIPAA certified' seal exists. HHS does not certify vendors. Third-party attestations (e.g., HITRUST CSF certification) are the industry standard proxy.

hitrust_csf.description: HITRUST Common Security Framework — the de facto healthcare compliance certification. Recognized by HHS as a recognized security framework.
hitrust_csf.recommendation: NOT recommended at LocalWeb's current stage. Pursue only if targeting hospital networks or health systems as direct clients.

certification_path.recommended_now: Obtain a healthcare attorney opinion letter confirming the architectural attestation is legally defensible. Cost: $1,500–$5,000. This is the minimum credibility investment.

gdpr.framework_summary: GDPR applies to any processing of personal data of EU/EEA residents, regardless of where the processor is located. Key roles: Controller (determines purpose/means), Processor (processes on controller's behalf), Sub-processor (processes on processor's behalf).
gdpr.localweb_role: LocalWeb acts as a DATA PROCESSOR when building/hosting websites for clients who collect EU visitor data. LocalWeb's hosting providers (Cloudflare, Netlify, Vercel) are SUB-PROCESSORS.

findings.claim: GDPR-ready websites
findings.rationale: LocalWeb CAN legitimately market websites as 'GDPR-ready' if the deliverable includes: (1) cookie consent banner, (2) privacy policy template, (3) DPA signed by LocalWeb as processor, (4) disclosure of sub-processors (Cloudflare, Formspree, etc.). 'GDPR-ready' is not a regulated term. However, actual GDPR compliance is the client's responsibility — LocalWeb provides the tools, the client must use them correctly.
findings.risk_level: MEDIUM — claim is marketable but requires DPA infrastructure

findings.claim: LocalWeb must sign DPAs with clients who have EU users
findings.rationale: GDPR Article 28 requires controllers to have a written DPA with every processor. If LocalWeb hosts a website for a client whose users include EU residents, LocalWeb IS a processor and MUST have a signed DPA. This is a legal requirement, not optional.
findings.required_action: Draft a standard DPA. Include: (a) purpose and duration of processing, (b) nature of personal data processed, (c) security measures, (d) sub-processor list, (e) breach notification obligations (72 hours to controller), (f) data deletion/return on contract end.
findings.risk_level: HIGH — non-compliance = potential €10M or 2% global turnover fine

findings.claim: Sub-processor disclosure: Cloudflare, Formspree, Netlify, Vercel
findings.rationale: LocalWeb must disclose all sub-processors in its DPA. Cloudflare maintains its own sub-processor list and GDPR DPA. Formspree has GDPR documentation. Netlify and Vercel both publish DPAs. LocalWeb must: (1) list all sub-processors, (2) notify clients 30 days before adding new sub-processors, (3) ensure each sub-processor has adequate GDPR safeguards.
findings.cloudflare_status: ISO 27701 certified, DPA available, sub-processor list published
findings.formspree_status: GDPR-compliant per their documentation; DPA available
findings.vercel_status: DPA available; controller/processor distinction depends on plan tier
findings.required_action: Build and maintain a published sub-processor list. Template available from sub-processor DPA pages.
findings.risk_level: MEDIUM — paperwork gap, not architectural gap

findings.claim: Cloudflare Workers processing EU data — transfer mechanism
findings.rationale: Cloudflare operates a global edge network. EU visitor data may be processed at non-EU edge nodes depending on routing. Cloudflare has EU data localization options. For clients requiring EU-only processing, this must be explicitly configured.
findings.required_action: Include data transfer disclosure in DPA. If EU-only processing is required, note this as a premium configuration.
findings.risk_level: MEDIUM for EU healthcare/legal clients

findings.claim: ISO 27701 certification supports GDPR-ready claim
findings.rationale: ISO 27701 (Privacy Information Management System) directly maps to GDPR requirements and is the strongest available third-party attestation. Cloudflare holds ISO 27701 certification. LocalWeb itself does not. Claiming 'GDPR-ready' based on Cloudflare's certification is permissible but must be clearly attributed — LocalWeb cannot claim Cloudflare's certifications as its own.
findings.risk_level: LOW if claims are accurately attributed

iso_27701.description: Privacy Information Management System — the primary GDPR-aligned certification
iso_27701.timeline: 3–9 months for ISO 27001; additional 3–6 months for 27701
iso_27701.recommendation: Phase 2 goal (12–18 months). ISO 27001 alone is highly marketable.

certification_path.recommended_now: Draft and execute DPA template. Publish sub-processor list. Cost: legal fees $2,000–$5,000 for template drafting.

ontario.note: Ontario is NOT subject to US HIPAA. Ontario health information is governed by PHIPA (Personal Health Information Protection Act, 2004). NAPRA governs pharmacy practice management systems. LSO governs law firm practice. These are distinct frameworks.

findings.claim: Ontario healthcare websites must comply with PHIPA, not HIPAA
findings.rationale: PHIPA is Ontario's health privacy law. It applies to 'health information custodians' (physicians, pharmacists, hospitals, etc.) and their agents. PHIPA is similar in structure to HIPAA but has differences: (a) breach notification threshold is lower — any intentional unauthorized access must be reported, vs HIPAA's 500-person threshold trigger; (b) PHIPA applies to ALL health information, not just 'unsecured' PHI; (c) the Information and Privacy Commissioner of Ontario (IPC) is the regulator, not HHS/OCR.
findings.implication: LocalWeb's 'HIPAA-ready' positioning is INCORRECT for Ontario clients. Must reframe as 'PHIPA-compliant architecture' for Canadian healthcare market.
findings.required_action: Update Ontario-facing marketing to reference PHIPA, not HIPAA. The architectural argument is the same — LocalWeb doesn't touch personal health information — but the legal framework referenced must be accurate.
findings.risk_level: HIGH — misrepresenting the applicable law to healthcare clients is a credibility/liability issue

findings.claim: NAPRA regulates pharmacy practice management systems, not pharmacy websites
findings.rationale: NAPRA's Practice Management Systems requirements (38 requirements, 2013 framework) govern the pharmacy's dispensing/clinical software — audit logging, secure messaging, data storage, remote access. These requirements apply to the pharmacy's core system, NOT to a patient-facing marketing website. LocalWeb's RxReady product interfaces with the pharmacy system but is not itself a Practice Management System.
findings.implication: LocalWeb does NOT need NAPRA PPMS compliance. The pharmacy's system must comply; LocalWeb connects to the API output only.
findings.required_action: Clarify in pharmacy-facing materials that RxReady is a patient-facing web interface, not a pharmacy management system, and is therefore outside NAPRA PPMS scope.
findings.risk_level: LOW — no NAPRA requirements apply to LocalWeb's product scope

findings.claim: CPSO (College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario) regulates physician advertising
findings.rationale: CPSO's Advertising Policy governs what Ontario physicians can say in their marketing materials. Restrictions include: no false/misleading claims, no before-and-after photos without consent/disclosure, no testimonials with unverifiable outcomes, no superlatives. This is the PHYSICIAN's obligation, not LocalWeb's. However, LocalWeb website builds for physician clients must accommodate these restrictions.
findings.implication: LocalWeb's medical practice website templates must be designed to be CPSO-compliant by default — no testimonial widgets, no outcome guarantee language, no 'best doctor in Toronto' copy. This is a template design requirement.
findings.required_action: Add CPSO advertising guidelines to medical practice website templates. Include a checklist for clients.
findings.risk_level: MEDIUM — if LocalWeb templates contain non-compliant elements, clients may face CPSO complaints

findings.claim: LSO (Law Society of Ontario) regulates law firm practice management but not website content directly
findings.rationale: LSO's Technology Guideline addresses when technology use is mandatory (e.g., electronic registration) and recommended best practices. LSO's By-Law 9 governs trust account management. As of 2025, LSO's mandatory contingency planning requirement (effective Jan 1, 2025) requires firms to designate an administrator for incapacity/death scenarios. LSO does not regulate website content directly, but its Rules of Professional Conduct prohibit misleading advertising by lawyers.
findings.implication: Law firm websites built by LocalWeb must not contain misleading claims, must not guarantee outcomes, and must display required disclosures (law firm name, contact, jurisdiction). These are the lawyer's obligations.
findings.required_action: Law firm website templates must include: proper firm identification, jurisdiction disclosure, no outcome guarantees, no 'best lawyer' claims. Add LSO advertising rules summary to client onboarding.
findings.risk_level: LOW for LocalWeb; MEDIUM for law firm clients if not guided

findings.claim: Ontario pharmacy patient-facing websites — PHIPA data handling
findings.rationale: Prescription status lookup using Rx number + DOB: under PHIPA, an Rx number combined with DOB may constitute personal health information because it can be used to identify a patient and relates to their health record. Ontario's IPC would likely view the Rx number + DOB lookup pair as PHI-adjacent, requiring the pharmacy (as health information custodian) to have a written agreement with LocalWeb as an 'agent' under PHIPA.
findings.required_action: For Ontario pharmacy clients: draft a PHIPA Agent Agreement (not a HIPAA BAA) confirming LocalWeb's role and data handling. The architectural argument still works — LocalWeb doesn't store the data — but the agreement must exist and reference PHIPA.
findings.risk_level: MEDIUM — Ontario IPC has enforcement authority; pharmacy could face compliance review

findings.claim: Canadian privacy law baseline: PIPEDA (federal) and Quebec Law 25
findings.rationale: Ontario commercial websites (non-health) are subject to PIPEDA (Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act) federally. Quebec customers face Law 25 (effective in full since Sept 2023), the most stringent privacy law in Canada — GDPR-equivalent requirements including mandatory privacy impact assessments, explicit consent, and 72-hour breach notification. If LocalWeb serves Quebec clients, a separate privacy framework review is warranted.
findings.required_action: Flag Quebec as a separate compliance tier in client onboarding.
findings.risk_level: MEDIUM for Quebec-based clients

findings.claim: Hash-chained audit trails support compliance evidence
findings.rationale: SHA-256 hash chains are the industry standard for tamper-evident audit logs. HIPAA's Security Rule (45 CFR 164.312(b)) requires audit controls — 'hardware, software, and/or procedural mechanisms that record and examine activity in information systems.' NIST SP 800-92 (Guide to Computer Security Log Management) endorses cryptographic integrity verification for audit logs. SOC 2's Common Criteria 7.2 (CC7.2) requires 'monitoring of system components and the operation of those components.' Hash-chained logs directly satisfy these requirements.
findings.precedent: Digital forensics in court proceedings routinely relies on MD5/SHA-256 hash verification to establish evidence integrity. FRE 901(b)(9) (Federal Rules of Evidence) accepts scientific process authentication, which hash chains satisfy.
findings.risk_level: LOW — well-established technical and legal precedent

findings.claim: Forensic CoC is a compliance differentiator LocalWeb can market
findings.rationale: LocalWeb's hash-manifest-based audit trail system is a genuine differentiator in the website-for-regulated-industries space. Most website builders offer zero forensic infrastructure. The ability to produce a cryptographically-verified history of every change to a website, with timestamps and content hashes, is valuable to: (a) compliance auditors conducting SOC 2 reviews, (b) legal clients needing evidence of website state at a specific date, (c) healthcare clients needing to demonstrate 'what did our site say on date X' in response to a patient complaint.
findings.limitation: LocalWeb's CoC covers WEBSITE CHANGES (design, content, configuration) — not patient data transactions. This distinction must be clear in marketing.
findings.risk_level: LOW — claim is accurate if scope is clearly stated

findings.claim: SOC 2 auditors will accept hash manifests as evidence
findings.rationale: SOC 2 Type II auditors accept any verifiable, tamper-evident audit mechanism. The AICPA's Trust Services Criteria do not mandate a specific technical format — they require that monitoring controls exist and produce evidence. A hash-chained JSONL log with signed entries is more rigorous than most off-the-shelf logging tools and will be accepted. However: the log must be complete (cover the entire audit period), must be retained (minimum 1 year for SOC 2), and must be producible on request.
findings.required_action: Implement log retention policy (minimum 12 months, preferably 24). Ensure logs cover all system changes, not just content changes.
findings.risk_level: LOW

findings.claim: Legal discovery value — 'what did our site say on date X'
findings.rationale: For law firm clients especially, being able to demonstrate the exact state of their website on any given date is legally valuable. Class action law firms, personal injury practices, and medical malpractice firms have been sued over website advertising claims. A hash-verified historical record of website content is court-admissible evidence under FRE 901. This is a distinct value proposition no generic website builder offers.
findings.risk_level: LOW — this is a genuine advantage
